units.translation: A similar adjective occurs at Ag. 1216 στροβει ταρασσων φροιμίοις εφημενους [whirling, troubling with preludes those who follow], where εφημενους [those who follow] has been introduced from the next verse by a copyist's error. Meineke Philol. vol. 20 p. 72 wanted φλογα [flame]. But he wanted a verse without the poet's name preserved by Aelian V. H. 13, 1. άσσουσα (read διάττουσα [darting through], which Cobet corrected Mnem. 7 p. 224, unless he wrote άτ-τουσα) δ᾽ ἐξέλαμψεν ἀστραπῆς δίκην [and flashing like lightning] he wanted to insert, rejected by Wecklein in Ritschl's Museum Rhen. new series vol. 28 p. 696. It is undoubtedly another verse of the poet, spoken about Diana, as can be gathered from Aelian's words.

Meineke Philol. vol. 20 p. 72 wanted φλογα [flame]. But he wanted a verse without the poet's name preserved by Aelian V. H. 13, 1. άσσουσα (read διάττουσα [darting through], which Cobet corrected Mnem. 7 p. 224, unless he wrote άτ-τουσα) δ᾽ ἐξέλαμψεν ἀστραπῆς δίκην [and flashing like lightning] he wanted to insert, rejected by Wecklein in Ritschl's Museum Rhen. new series vol. 28 p. 696. It is undoubtedly another verse of the poet, spoken about Diana, as can be gathered from Aelian's words.
Πολλά [many things] either joined with a substantive or used substantively without a noun.
Not rarely two cases of this adjective are placed in one sentence.
Πολύς [much] joined with other adjectives with καί [and] interposed,
And πολλά [many things] with an adjective joined by itself
Πολύ [much] and πολλῷ [by much] with comparatives and superlatives
Adverbially πολλά [many things] in many ways, often.
πολύς [much] so used that it signifies the same thing happening more often.
The forms πολλός [much], which Sophocles and Euripides sometimes used, have no examples in Aeschylus.
Ρεῖ πολὺς ὅδε [This one flows abundantly]
Πολὺς πλούτου λιμὴν, ὡς ἐν μιᾷ πληγῇ κατέφθαρται [A great harbor of wealth, how it has been destroyed in one blow]

where the first πολύς [much] is suspect, not so much because of the repeated πολύς [much] in the next verse πολὺς ὄλβος [great wealth], although this too has something offensive, but because there was no reason why he should say πολὺς πλούτου λιμήν [a great harbor of wealth], when μέγας πλούτου λιμήν [a great harbor of wealth] was ready, which Euripides said Or. 1077 ὦ δῶμα πατρὸς καὶ μέγας πλούτου λιμήν [O house of my father and great harbor of wealth]. This therefore seems to Nauck in Mélanges Gréco-Romains vol. 3. a. 1871 p. 295 to be restored to Aeschylus too, and that all the more because πολύς [much] for μέγας [great] is characteristic of Byzantine rather than ancient Greek. But rightly said
Πολὺς πλούτου [A great harbor of wealth]
Meineke's conjecture is worthy of consideration: ταύς πλούτου λιμήν [a great harbor of wealth], about which see vol. 2 p. 6.
